  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qiming Zhu
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:qimingzhu@link.cuhk.edu.cn">qimingzhu@link.cuhk.edu.cn</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shunian Chen
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Benyou Wang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Long-horizon agents often compress interaction histories into write-time summaries. This creates a fundamental <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">write-before-query</span> barrier: compression decisions are made before the system knows what a future query will hinge on. As a result, summaries can cause <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">unverifiable omissions</span>—decisive constraints (e.g., allergies) may be dropped, leaving the agent unable to justify an answer with traceable evidence. Retaining raw logs restores an authoritative source of truth, but grounding on raw logs by default is expensive: many queries are answerable from summaries, yet raw grounding still requires processing far longer contexts, inflating token consumption and latency.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We propose <span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TierMem</span>, a provenance-linked framework that casts retrieval as an inference-time evidence allocation problem. TierMem uses a <span id="abstract1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">two-tier</span> memory hierarchy to answer with the <em id="abstract1.2.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cheapest sufficient evidence</em>: it queries a fast summary index by default, and a runtime <span id="abstract1.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sufficiency router</span> <span id="abstract1.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalates</span> to an immutable raw-log store only when summary evidence is insufficient. TierMem then writes back verified findings as new summary units linked to their raw sources. On LoCoMo, TierMem achieves <span id="abstract1.2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.851</span> accuracy (vs. <span id="abstract1.2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.873</span> raw-only) while reducing input tokens by <span id="abstract1.2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">54.1%</span> and latency by <span id="abstract1.2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">60.7%</span>. Code is available at <a href="https://github.com/FreedomIntelligence/Tiermem" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/FreedomIntelligence/Tiermem</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>LLM Agents, Agent Memory, Hierarchical Memory, Routing, GRPO, Cost-Aware Optimization
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Long-horizon language agents increasingly need to answer over interaction histories spanning weeks or months <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
At scale, their memory must be simultaneously <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">evidence-faithful</em> (grounded in source), <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">auditable</em> (traceable to provenance), and <em id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">economical</em> (low latency and cost).
Yet most current systems rely on <em id="S1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">write-time compression</em> into summaries or extracted facts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chhikara et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, committing to what to retain <em id="S1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">before</em> the agent knows what future queries will require.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summaries at write-time may erase decisive evidence.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Write-time compression forces irreversible retention decisions under uncertainty, requiring a preemptive bet on saliency before the query distribution is known <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Consequently, even state-of-the-art summarizers discard nuances that later prove decisive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
For instance, compressing a “severe peanut allergy” into generic “dietary preferences” creates an <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">unverifiable omission</span>: when later asked “Is this snack safe?”, the agent cannot trace or cite the specific constraint from its memory.
Thus, any fixed-budget summary admits a worst-case query it cannot support with traceable evidence. These failures are not merely occasional summarization errors; they are structural risks of lossy, write-before-query compression.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Raw grounding is auditable but often wasteful.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural response is to avoid compression and always ground on raw logs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Asai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
This improves auditability, but it is often economically and algorithmically inefficient.
Naively feeding long histories or globally retrieving large raw contexts incurs substantial token and latency costs, and long inputs can even degrade effective context utilization due to position-sensitive failures and attention dilution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Crucially, most queries do <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> require raw-level evidence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bridging the gap: Answer with the cheapest sufficient evidence.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These two extremes suggest that long-horizon memory access should be <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">query-conditioned</em>.
Given a query, the agent should retrieve the <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lowest-cost</em> memory granularity that still provides <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sufficient evidence</em> for faithful, auditable answering. This principle echoes recent adaptive RAG work that selectively accesses external evidence to trade off quality against retrieval cost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
We view this as an <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">inference-time evidence allocation problem</span>: decide at runtime when cheap summaries are enough and when the system must consult authoritative raw sources.
A practical system must therefore (i) detect when retrieved summaries are evidence-insufficient, (ii) fall back to an auditable source of truth only in those cases, and (iii) consolidate verified findings back into cheap memory to amortize future queries.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">TierMem: linked summaries with selective escalation.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Drawing inspiration from tiered caches, we propose <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TierMem</span>, a linked two-tier memory hierarchy governed by a runtime sufficiency check.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, Tier-1 is a fast summary index whose units are <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">explicitly linked</em> to their source raw pages via provenance pointers, enabling targeted escalation.
Tier-2 is an immutable raw-log store that serves as an auditable source of truth.
Given a user query, TierMem first retrieves from Tier-1 and applies a lightweight <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">miss detector</span> (router) that judges whether the retrieved summary evidence is sufficient.
On a <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">hit</span>, the agent answers immediately from summaries.
On a <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">miss</span>, the system <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalates</span> to the linked raw pages (and, if needed, bounded global retrieval) for deep grounding.
After escalation, TierMem performs <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">verified write-back</span>: it distills only <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">grounded</em> evidence into new Tier-1 units linked back to supporting raw pages, enabling <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.9" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">online consolidation</em> without sacrificing auditability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across two long-horizon conversational memory benchmarks, <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LoCoMo</span> and <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LongMemEval</span>, TierMem nearly matches raw-only accuracy while substantially reducing query-time cost by escalating only when necessary.
On <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LoCoMo</span>, TierMem reaches <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.851</span> accuracy versus <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.873</span> for always-raw, while reducing average input tokens by <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">54.1%</span> and latency by <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">60.7%</span> (3,396 vs. 7,398 tokens; 6.76s vs. 17.18s).
On <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LongMemEval</span>, where summary-only methods degrade sharply under long-range updates, TierMem mitigates compression loss by routing evidence-insufficient cases to raw grounding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h5>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem formulation.</span> We identify the <em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">write-before-query barrier</em> in summary-centric agent memory and cast long-horizon memory access as <em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inference-time evidence allocation</em>: choose the minimal granularity that provides sufficient evidence for faithful, auditable answering.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Framework.</span> We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TierMem</span>, a linked two-tier memory hierarchy with (i) <em id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">provenance-linked summaries</em>, (ii) a lightweight <em id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">miss detector</em> that routes <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> vs. <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span>, and (iii) <em id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">verified write-back</em> for online consolidation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empirics.</span> We show TierMem improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off on long-horizon benchmarks, recovering much of the benefit of raw grounding at substantially lower token and latency cost.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17913v1/frame.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/149;" width="476" height="149"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TierMem overview.<span id="S1.F1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> TierMem maintains a provenance-linked two-tier memory hierarchy.
Tier-1 is a fast summary index whose entries store (i) compact summaries and (ii) provenance links <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> to supporting Tier-2 raw pages in an immutable paged log.
Given a query, TierMem retrieves Tier-1 evidence and uses a lightweight router <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to choose <span id="S1.F1.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> (summaries only) or <span id="S1.F1.7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span> (consult linked raw pages, then run a bounded retrieval procedure if needed).
After escalation, TierMem can optionally perform verified write-back to update Tier-1 with evidence-backed findings linked to their raw sources.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>The TierMem Framework</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section introduces <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TierMem</span>, a two-tier memory framework that casts long-horizon retrieval as an <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inference-time evidence allocation</em> problem.
TierMem prioritizes efficiency by defaulting to a fast summary tier, yet eliminates unverifiable omissions by <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalating</span> to immutable raw logs when summaries lack sufficient detail.
Crucially, the system employs a <em id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">provenance-linked</em> architecture to ensure that all consolidated memories remain traceable to their source.Detailed architectural design and implementation specifics are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Architecture: Provenance-Linked 2 Tier Memory</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TierMem organizes memory into two distinct levels of granularity, bridged by <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">explicit provenance links</span> to ensure traceability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tier-2: Immutable Paged Raw Log (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{R}</annotation></semantics></math>).</span>
To guarantee auditability, Tier-2 stores the full interaction history as immutable, fixed-size pages (e.g., <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1000 tokens), each assigned a stable identifier.
Unlike sliding windows, paged storage ensures that evidence units remain static, allowing stable citation even as the context grows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tier-1: Provenance Index (<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{S}</annotation></semantics></math>).</span>
Tier-1 acts as a semantic cache for fast retrieval.
Each entry contains: (i) a concise summary, (ii) a dense embedding for retrieval, and (iii) <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">provenance links</span> (<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) pointing to the specific Tier-2 page identifiers that support the summary.
These links prevent hallucinations by anchoring summaries to raw data and provide a high-recall “warm start” pointer during escalation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Construction.</span>
The tiers are built synchronously: whenever a raw page is sealed in Tier-2, TierMem synthesizes corresponding summary entries in Tier-1, automatically recording the links <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. This ensures no summary exists without a traceable raw source.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Inference Protocol: Adaptive Routing and Consolidation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a query, TierMem executes a dynamic protocol (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) to select the minimal sufficient evidence granularity.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Router Policy (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>).</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The core decision maker is a lightweight policy <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> that judges <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">evidence sufficiency</em>.
It takes the query and retrieved Tier-1 summaries as input and outputs a binary decision: <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> or <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span>.
The policy is trained to define “sufficiency” strictly: it must escalate if the summary lacks precise constraints (e.g., negations, exact values, attribution) required for a faithful answer (training details in §<a href="#S3" title="3 Router Optimization ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Phase 1: Fast Path (Default).</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TierMem first retrieves top-<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> summaries from Tier-1.
If <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> outputs <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span>, the system generates the response immediately using only these summaries.
This path minimizes latency and cost for the majority of queries where high-level context suffices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Phase 2: Provenance-Guided Escalation.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> outputs <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span>, TierMem triggers a <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bounded retrieval loop</span> to recover missing details.
Crucially, this search is <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">provenance-guided</em>: it prioritizes reading the Tier-2 pages explicitly linked (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) by the retrieved summaries, as these likely contain the omitted nuances.
If this initial look-up remains insufficient, the system performs a limited multi-hop search over Tier-2 (up to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{max}</annotation></semantics></math> steps) to locate disconnected evidence.
This ensures deep grounding without the prohibitive cost of reading the full raw history.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Phase 3: Verified Write-Back.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To prevent recurring escalations for the same topic, TierMem performs <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">online consolidation</span>.
After a successful escalation, the system extracts the newly verified details and updates Tier-1 via a <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">retrieve-and-edit</em> operation: new findings are either added as new entries or merged into existing ones.
Importantly, these updates preserve the provenance links to the Tier-2 evidence used during escalation, maintaining the chain of custody.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Router Optimization</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We optimize the router <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to minimize inference costs while maintaining the accuracy of a raw-grounded upper bound.The full experimental setup for router training is detailed in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Router: Data Construction, Training Pipeline, and Hyperparameters ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Training Signal: Summary Sufficiency Labels</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We supervise <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> using a <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">hindsight labeling</span> strategy.
For a given query, we generate two answers: (1) a <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Summary-Only</em> answer, and (2) a <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Raw-Grounded</em> answer (derived from the escalation path).
An LLM judge compares these against the query requirements:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Label <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> (0): If the summary-only answer is correct and complete.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Label <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span> (1): If the summary answer is vague or incorrect, but the raw-grounded answer recovers the necessary details.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This filters out “impossible” queries (where even raw logs fail) and isolates cases where write-time compression caused an unverifiable omission.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Optimization: Distillation and Alignment</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ a two-stage training process to refine the decision boundary.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 1: Distillation (SFT).</span>
We distill routing behavior from a stronger teacher (<span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-5</span>) that outputs a short rationale and the final decision. We fine-tune the router to imitate the teacher outputs, keeping only examples where the teacher decision matches our oracle label (details in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Stage 1: SFT via GPT-5 Thinking+Action Distillation ‣ Appendix B Router: Data Construction, Training Pipeline, and Hyperparameters ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 2: Cost-Aware Alignment (GRPO).</span>
To explicitly manage the accuracy-efficiency trade-off, we further optimize <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The reward function is defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{acc}}(\tau)\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{cost}}R_{\mathrm{cost}}(\tau)\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{waste}}R_{\mathrm{waste}}(\tau)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>acc</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>cost</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>cost</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>waste</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>waste</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{acc}}(\tau)\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{cost}}R_{\mathrm{cost}}(\tau)\;-\;\lambda_{\mathrm{waste}}R_{\mathrm{waste}}(\tau)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>acc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math> rewards answer correctness, <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{cost}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>cost</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{cost}}</annotation></semantics></math> penalizes the computational cost of escalation, and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{waste}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>waste</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{waste}}</annotation></semantics></math> specifically penalizes “false alarms” (escalating when summaries were actually sufficient).
This objective forces the model to escalate only when the expected gain in faithfulness outweighs the retrieval cost.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We reframe memory retrieval as a problem of <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">inference-time evidence allocation</span>.
Our central hypothesis is that aligning retrieval granularity with query complexity—defaulting to efficient summaries and <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalating</span> to raw logs only when strictly necessary—can break the static trade-off between cost and faithfulness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate whether TierMem successfully navigates this optimization landscape through four Research Questions (RQs):</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<dl id="S4.I1" class="ltx_description" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0cm;">
<dt id="S4.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1 (Trade-off):</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does TierMem improve the accuracy–efficiency trade-off compared to static summary-only and raw-only policies?</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S4.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2 (Control Mechanism):</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Can a lightweight router reliably detect evidence insufficiency (distinguishing <span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> vs. <span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span>) with negligible inference overhead?</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S4.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3 (Structural Utility):</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Do explicit provenance pointers (Tier-1<math id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Tier-2) measurably improve the grounding quality of escalated queries?</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S4.I1.ix4" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ4 (Online Amortization):</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Does the consolidation of verified findings reduce future cache misses, effectively amortizing raw-access costs over time?</p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Baselines</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare against representative systems spanning summary-centric and raw/controller-centric paradigms.
On the summary-centric side, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mem0</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chhikara et al., 2025</a>)</cite> <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LightMem</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">O-mem</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemOS</span>  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite> primarily rely on compact written memories for fast retrieval.
On the raw/controller-centric side, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MemR3</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GAM</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> allocate more inference-time budget to access fine-grained evidence and improve grounding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For TierMem, we report:
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (summary)</span> (Tier-1 only),
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (raw-data)</span> (always Tier-2),
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (router)</span> (learned routing),
and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (router, GPT-4.1-mini)</span> (a stronger LLM routing reference). To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, we <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">disable online write-back</span> for all methods in the main benchmark evaluation. We use GPT-4.1-mini as the backbone in memory systems.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Fair comparison within TierMem.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To isolate <em id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">memory access policy</em> from model choice, all TierMem variants use the same generator, the same embedding model for Tier-1 dense retrieval, and the same reranker.
Among TierMem variants, the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">only</span> differences are (i) whether Tier-2 is consulted, and (ii) how/when escalation is triggered (always vs. routed).
We report efficiency measured in the QA phase (retrieval + generation) and explicitly account for routing overhead when present.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Metrics and Cost Accounting</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report both <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">answer quality</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">query-time efficiency</span>, together with <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">routing behavior</span> and a specific metric for compression loss.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Answer quality &amp; Compression Loss.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report:
(i) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-judge accuracy</span> (primary): fraction of queries judged correct by the benchmark protocol.
(ii) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unverifiable Omission Rate (UOR)</span>: To quantify the write-before-query barrier, we measure the fraction of queries where summary-based methods fail specifically due to missing evidence (i.e., the answer can be found in our raw-data system but was lost in summaries), distinguishing these from reasoning failures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Query-time efficiency (QA phase).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure:
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg. input tokens / query</span> (Tok<math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>in</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{in}}</annotation></semantics></math>/Q),
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg. output tokens / query</span> (Tok<math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>out</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math>/Q),
and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg. latency / query</span> (Lat./Q), when measured.
Unless otherwise stated, escalation uses a bounded Deep Search Loop capped at <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\max}{=}3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\max}{=}3</annotation></semantics></math> iterations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Routing behavior.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure:
(i) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R-rate</span> (fraction of queries routed to <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span>),
(ii) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Recall on hard cases</span> (fraction of oracle-hard queries correctly escalated),
and (iii) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Router overhead</span> (tokens consumed by the routing step itself).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Token accounting for routed systems.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For routed variants, we decompose query-time token usage into:
<math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Tok}_{\text{in}}=\text{Tok}_{\text{QA}}+\text{Tok}_{\text{router}}\quad\text{Tok}_{\text{out}}=\text{Tok}_{\text{gen}}+\text{Tok}_{\text{router-out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>QA</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>router</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>router-out</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Tok}_{\text{in}}=\text{Tok}_{\text{QA}}+\text{Tok}_{\text{router}}\quad\text{Tok}_{\text{out}}=\text{Tok}_{\text{gen}}+\text{Tok}_{\text{router-out}}</annotation></semantics></math>
and report both the total and the components (where applicable).
This makes the cost–fidelity trade-off explicit: routing should reduce <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Tok}_{\text{QA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>QA</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Tok}_{\text{QA}}</annotation></semantics></math> by avoiding unnecessary raw reads, while keeping <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Tok}_{\text{router}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>Tok</mtext><mtext>router</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Tok}_{\text{router}}</annotation></semantics></math> small.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results: Accuracy–Efficiency trade-off</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the accuracy–efficiency trade-off (RQ1) across both benchmarks.
Broadly, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (summary)</span> is the most efficient but suffers from compression loss (the <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">write-before-query barrier</span>), while <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (raw-data)</span> is the most accurate but costly.
<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (router)</span> balances this via <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">inference-time evidence allocation</span>, approaching raw-only accuracy with summary-like efficiency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LoCoMo.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The write-before-query barrier is quantifiable via UOR analysis (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ LongMemEval. ‣ 4.2 Main Results: Accuracy–Efficiency trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>): summary-centric baselines exhibit high omission rates (14.7%–23.3%), confirming that errors often stem from evidence unavailability.
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (router)</span> overcomes this, achieving <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.851</span> overall accuracy (approaching the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">0.873</span> raw-only upper bound) while reducing average input tokens by <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">54.1%</span> and latency by <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">60.7%</span> compared to the raw baseline.
In contrast, <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (summary)</span> drops to 0.755 accuracy, consistent with its 15.4% UOR.
The router provides the largest gains on queries requiring precise details (e.g., entities, temporal qualifiers) that static summaries often drop.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LongMemEval.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ LongMemEval. ‣ 4.2 Main Results: Accuracy–Efficiency trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the summary-raw gap widens due to long-range dependencies.
Static summaries fail to retain answerable evidence for nearly 30% of queries (e.g., 29.6% UOR for Mem0).
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ours (router)</span> effectively bridges this gap by selectively escalating hard cases, offering a superior trade-off compared to static memory formats.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>LoCoMo test results. <span id="S4.T1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UOR (Unverifiable Omission Rate)</span> quantifies errors caused by missing evidence in summaries (lower is better). Bold indicates the best result in each column.</figcaption>

<thead class="ltx_thead">

</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why routing helps.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A routed system is a mixture of two regimes: the cheap <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> path (Tier-1 only) and the expensive <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span> path (Tier-2 grounding).
The goal is therefore not to maximize escalation, but to:
(i) achieve high accuracy on the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> path when summaries are semantically sufficient,
and (ii) reliably trigger <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Escalate</span> when summaries are underspecified or high-risk. By dynamically detecting insufficiency, TierMem effectively converts the high UOR observed in baselines (15-30%) into recoverable cases via provenance-guided escalation.
We quantify this in §<a href="#S5" title="5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Analysis and Ablations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze how TierMem achieves its accuracy–efficiency trade-off and isolate the contributions of its key mechanisms.
We focus on routing behavior (RQ2), provenance pointers (RQ3), and online consolidation (RQ4), and conclude with error analysis.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Routing Behavior Breakdown</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On LoCoMo, the final router (SFT+GRPO) escalates <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">39.0%</span> of queries and recalls <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">71.7%</span> of oracle-hard cases (Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ End-to-end impact. ‣ 5.2 Router Learning and Cost–Fidelity Trade-off ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Routing overhead is <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">678 tokens/query</span> on average, decomposed as <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">584</span> input and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">94.5</span> output tokens (Tok<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}_{\text{in}}{=}3396.4{+}584" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3396.4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>584</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{in}}{=}3396.4{+}584</annotation></semantics></math>, Tok<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}_{\text{out}}{=}247.7{+}94.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>247.7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>94.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{out}}{=}247.7{+}94.5</annotation></semantics></math>; Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ LongMemEval. ‣ 4.2 Main Results: Accuracy–Efficiency trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
This corresponds to <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">14.7%</span> of total input tokens (584/3980.4) and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">15.7%</span> of total tokens (678/4322.6) per query.
We analyze how training improves this routing boundary in §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Router Learning and Cost–Fidelity Trade-off ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Router Learning and Cost–Fidelity Trade-off</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To isolate the impact of router training (RQ2), we compare several router variants in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ End-to-end impact. ‣ 5.2 Router Learning and Cost–Fidelity Trade-off ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
We report both <em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mechanism metrics</em> (routing classification) and <em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">outcome metrics</em> (end-to-end QA).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training stages improve both behavior and overhead.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-shot</span> router is not only less accurate, but also inefficient due to poor protocol adherence, producing excessive output tokens.
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SFT</span> regularizes the output format and establishes basic routing logic, improving recall on hard queries while reducing overhead.
<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SFT+GRPO</span> further sharpens the decision boundary: it improves hard-case recall to <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">71.7%</span> and achieves the best local routing F1-score, indicating that RL improves discrimination rather than merely escalating more.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">End-to-end impact.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite a small routing overhead (Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ End-to-end impact. ‣ 5.2 Router Learning and Cost–Fidelity Trade-off ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SFT+GRPO</span> matches the stronger GPT-4.1-mini router in overall LoCoMo accuracy (0.851) and reduces latency substantially compared to raw-only.
These results support the core premise of TierMem: a lightweight router can act as a semantic cache controller, allocating expensive raw evidence only when needed.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span><span id="S5.T3.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Impact of Training Strategies on Router Behavior.</span>
<span id="S5.T3.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Router Cost</span> denotes the average token overhead (Input+Output) incurred by the routing step itself.
The <span id="S5.T3.22" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-shot</span> baseline is inefficient, generating excessive output tokens (<math id="S5.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>317 avg output) due to poor instruction following.
<span id="S5.T3.23" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SFT</span> regularizes the output format, reducing overhead to <math id="S5.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>678 tokens.
<span id="S5.T3.24" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SFT+GRPO</span> achieves the best performance trade-off: for a negligible router overhead (<math id="S5.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>678 tokens), it recovers <span id="S5.T3.25" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">71.7%</span> of hard queries and matches GPT-4.1-mini’s accuracy, effectively saving 51% of total system costs compared to the Raw-only upper bound. Additional analysis of S/R counterfactual outcomes and why similar end-to-end accuracy can arise despite different hard-case recall is provided in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Additional Analysis: Why Higher Hard-Recall Can Tie on End-to-End Judge Score ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
</figcaption>
<div id="S5.T3.26" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:56.1pt;vertical-align:-26.8pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-128.9pt,21.0pt) scale(0.572382577108889,0.572382577108889) ;">

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablation: Effect of Provenance Pointers</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key design choice in TierMem is explicit Tier-1<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Tier-2 provenance linking, used to warm-start escalation on likely relevant raw pages (RQ3).
We compare:
(i) <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linked</span>, full TierMem with provenance pointers enabled, and
(ii) <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No-Linked</span>, an otherwise identical system where escalation performs global retrieval (BM25) without prioritizing linked raw pages.
Results are shown in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Overall accuracy improves via better escalations. ‣ 5.3 Ablation: Effect of Provenance Pointers ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overall accuracy improves via better escalations.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Provenance pointers yield a consistent end-to-end gain: <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linked</span> achieves <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">85.1%</span> accuracy compared to <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">83.6%</span> for <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No-Linked</span> (+1.5pp), with similar routing rates.
Crucially, improvements concentrate on escalated queries: <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Acc.@R</span> rises from <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">77.5%</span> to <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">81.7%</span> (+4.2pp), while the <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Answer</span> path remains unchanged.
This matches the intended causal role of provenance pointers: they do not change what summaries contain, but they improve how quickly and reliably the system finds decisive Tier-2 evidence when summaries are insufficient.A more detailed breakdown of escalation behaviors and retrieval dynamics is provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Detailed Analysis of Provenance Pointer Ablation ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S5.T5.11.1.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.9pt 9.0pt;">1,063 <span id="S5.T5.11.1.9.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">(+57)</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.11.1.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 9.0pt;">2,447</td>
<td id="S5.T5.11.1.9.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.9pt 9.0pt;">3.85</td>
<td id="S5.T5.11.1.9.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 9.0pt;">426</td>
<td id="S5.T5.11.1.9.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 9.0pt;">77</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Consolidation Over Replay Epochs</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TierMem supports continual improvement via <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">consolidation</span> (verified write-back).
For consistency with the benchmark protocol, we evaluate consolidation in an epoch-wise replay setting:
within each epoch, Tier-1 remains <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">fixed</span> while answering the full query set, and verified findings collected from escalations are written back <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">between</span> epochs.
This isolates the effect of consolidation on future queries while keeping per-epoch evaluation conditions identical (RQ4).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After a cache miss, TierMem escalates to Tier-2 to gather auditable evidence, then distills only <em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">verified</em> findings into Tier-1 as compact units <em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">linked</em> back to supporting raw pages.
Unlike generic summarization, write-back is <em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">query-triggered</em> and <em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">evidence-backed</em>: the system only commits what was needed and validated during escalation, revealing which details must persist under the write-before-query asymmetry.
In our implementation, the write-back controller supports three operations: <span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ADD</span>, <span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UPDATE</span>, and <span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SKIP</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Replay protocol (epoch-wise).</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a longitudinal study over three <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">replay epochs</span> using the same fixed query set.
Within each epoch, Tier-1 is <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">frozen</span>: answers are produced without modifying memory.
During the epoch, we <em id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">log</em> the verified findings extracted from escalations.
After the epoch finishes, we apply these logged updates in a <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">single batch</span> to produce the next Tier-1 state for the following replay epoch.
We evaluate (i) overall task accuracy, (ii) the fraction of queries routed to the cheap Summary path (Tier-1 only), and (iii) efficiency (average input tokens and latency).
If consolidation is effective, later replay epochs should answer more queries from Tier-1 <em id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">without losing correctness</em>, reducing the need for expensive raw grounding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Two write-back variants.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare two batch write-back strategies that differ in whether they <em id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">recall</em> existing related Tier-1 units before committing a new fact:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No-Recall write-back (E1–E3):</span> after completing an epoch, the system decides whether to write a new Tier-1 unit based only on each verified finding and its triggering query, without retrieving related Tier-1 units. If it writes, it always performs <span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ADD</span> (otherwise <span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SKIP</span>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Retrieve-and-Edit write-back (E1U–E3U):</span> after completing an epoch, the system first retrieves semantically related Tier-1 units using each verified finding as a query, then chooses among <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ADD/UPDATE/SKIP</span>. This enables <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UPDATE</span> and avoids uncontrolled growth of redundant entries.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results: consolidation increases cheap-path coverage and amortizes raw cost across replays.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Overall accuracy improves via better escalations. ‣ 5.3 Ablation: Effect of Provenance Pointers ‣ 5 Analysis and Ablations ‣ From Lossy to Verified: A Provenance-Aware Tiered Memory for Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes the evolution.
Across replay epochs, overall accuracy remains stable, yet the system answers more queries on the cheap summary path:
<span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S-Traffic</span> increases monotonically, and <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S-Correct</span> rises by <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">32%</span> (819<math id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math>1,083) under No-Recall write-back.
This indicates that as Tier-1 accumulates verified units <em id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">from prior replays</em>, a growing fraction of queries become answerable with sufficient evidence from summaries alone, offloading work that previously required raw-page reads.
Correspondingly, average token usage and latency decrease over time (e.g., Tok<math id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{avg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>avg</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{avg}}</annotation></semantics></math>: 3,958<math id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math>2,419; Latency: 5.14s<math id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\to" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\to</annotation></semantics></math>3.39s), demonstrating clear amortization of raw-access cost under repeated query demand.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Retrieve-and-Edit improves consolidation hygiene.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieve-and-Edit exhibits a similar trend of increasing Summary-path coverage, while maintaining overall accuracy at least as well as No-Recall at later epochs (e.g., 0.852 at E2U vs. 0.847 at E2).
Because it explicitly recalls related Tier-1 units, it can <span id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UPDATE</span> rather than blindly append, reducing semantic duplication and keeping Tier-1 more coherent.
This comes with a modest management overhead: Tok<math id="S5.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{\text{avg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>avg</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{\text{avg}}</annotation></semantics></math> decreases substantially, while latency can be slightly higher than No-Recall at the same epoch due to the additional recall-and-edit step.
Overall, Retrieve-and-Edit provides better consolidation hygiene while still enabling strong amortization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T6" class="ltx_table">
